title: Cauchy--Green reproduction of compactly supported test functions
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] and planar Lebesgue measure $dA$. Put $k(w)=1/(\pi w)$ for $w\neq0$ and $k(0)=0$. The function $k$ is locally integrable (its norm is integrable on every compact subset of $\mathbf C$). For every smooth $u:\mathbf C\to\mathbf C$ with compact support (the closure of its nonzero locus is compact) and every $z\in\mathbf C$, $$\int_{\mathbf C} k(z-\zeta)\frac{\partial u}{\partial\bar\zeta}(\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)=u(z),\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial\bar\zeta}=\frac12\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right),\quad\zeta=x+iy.$$ The integral is absolutely convergent; the value of the integrand at $\zeta=z$ is immaterial.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf. I section 3.A, formula (3.2) and proof, printed p.21: take a disk with boundary disjoint from supp u and reverse the denominator. Corollary (3.4) identifies the locally integrable kernel.

proof.text: For $c\in\mathbf C$, $s>0$, put $q_{c,s}(w)=|w-c|^{-1}$ when $0<|w-c|\leq s$, and zero otherwise. This is measurable. Apply the nonnegative polar formula to $q_{c,s}$: the Jacobian $r$ cancels $1/r$, leaving the indicator of $(0,s]\times(-\pi,\pi)$, whose product Lebesgue integral is $2\pi s$. Thus $q_{c,s}$ is integrable and $\int q_{c,s}\,dA=2\pi s$. The same polar formula applied to the indicator of a centered singleton or a centered circle gives area zero (the corresponding radial set is empty or a singleton). For every compact $K\subset\mathbf C$, choose $s$ with $K\subset\{|w|\leq s\}$; the measurable function $1_Kk$ has norm at most $q_{0,s}/\pi$. The majorant lemma proves its integrability, so $k$ is locally integrable. This also establishes that changing its chosen pole value changes no integral.

source.place: WANTED: I §3.A, formula (3.2) proof, printed p.21. Agent argument; source not accessible during this split.

proof.text: Fix $u,z$ and write $g=\partial_{\bar\zeta}u$. Outside the compact support $K_u$, $u$ is zero on a neighborhood, hence so are all its derivatives. Thus $g$ vanishes outside $K_u$ and, being continuous on $K_u$, is bounded there by a finite $M\geq0$. Choose $R>0$ with $K_u\subset\{|\zeta-z|<R\}$. Define $F(\zeta)=g(\zeta)/(z-\zeta)$ for $\zeta\ne z$ and $F(z)=0$. It is measurable and $|F|\leq Mq_{z,R}$; the majorant lemma and step 1 imply absolute convergence of $I=\int F\,dA$. The integral in the statement is $I/\pi$, and its pole value is immaterial by step 1.

source.place: WANTED: I §3.A, formula (3.2) proof, printed p.21. Agent argument; source not accessible during this split.

proof.text: For $0<\epsilon<R$, set $A_{\epsilon,R}=\{\epsilon\leq|\zeta-z|\leq R\}$ and $v(\zeta)=u(\zeta)/(z-\zeta)$ on $\mathbf C\setminus\{z\}$. This is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the closed annulus. Direct differentiation gives $\partial_x(z-\zeta)^{-1}=(z-\zeta)^{-2}$ and $\partial_y(z-\zeta)^{-1}=i(z-\zeta)^{-2}$, so $\partial_{\bar\zeta}(z-\zeta)^{-1}=0$ and $\partial_{\bar\zeta}v=F$. The annulus lemma applies with center $z$. Since $u=0$ on the outer circle, it yields $$A_\epsilon:=\int_{A_{\epsilon,R}}F\,dA=-\frac1{2i}\oint_{|\zeta-z|=\epsilon}\frac{u(\zeta)}{z-\zeta}\,d\zeta.$$

source.place: WANTED: I §3.A, formula (3.2) proof, printed p.21. Agent argument; source not accessible during this split.

proof.text: Parametrize the inner circle by $\zeta=z+\epsilon e^{it}$. Since $d\zeta=i\epsilon e^{it}dt$ and $z-\zeta=-\epsilon e^{it}$, step 3 becomes $A_\epsilon=\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}u(z+\epsilon e^{it})dt$. Let $\omega(\epsilon)=\sup_{0\leq t\leq2\pi}|u(z+\epsilon e^{it})-u(z)|$, finite by continuity on the compact interval. The majorant estimate for the interval measure gives $|A_\epsilon-\pi u(z)|\leq\pi\omega(\epsilon)$. Continuity at $z$ implies $\omega(\epsilon)\to0$: given $\delta>0$, choose $\eta>0$ so $|w-z|<\eta$ implies $|u(w)-u(z)|<\delta$; then every point of a circle of radius $\epsilon<\eta$ satisfies this bound and $\omega(\epsilon)\leq\delta$.

source.place: WANTED: I §3.A, formula (3.2) proof, printed p.21. Agent argument; source not accessible during this split.

proof.text: The support of $F$ lies in $\{|\zeta-z|<R\}$, and the circle and singleton exceptional sets have area zero by step 1. Splitting the absolutely convergent integral into the annulus and the inner disk therefore gives $I-A_\epsilon=\int_{|\zeta-z|<\epsilon}F\,dA$. Its integrand, extended by zero, is bounded in norm by $Mq_{z,\epsilon}$. The polar calculation and majorant estimate give $$|I-A_\epsilon|\leq M\int q_{z,\epsilon}\,dA=2\pi M\epsilon.$$

source.place: WANTED: I §3.A, formula (3.2) proof, printed p.21. Agent argument; source not accessible during this split.

proof.text: The triangle inequality combines steps 4 and 5 into $|I-\pi u(z)|\leq2\pi M\epsilon+\pi\omega(\epsilon)$ for every $0<\epsilon<R$. The right side tends to zero, so $I=\pi u(z)$. Dividing by $\pi$ proves the required reproduction identity, with the absolute convergence and pole-value assertion already proved in steps 1–2.
